stories.title: South Korea's 8.4GW AI data center buildout faces internal power design bottleneck
stories.summary: South Korea is pushing ahead with plans for roughly 8.4GW of AI data center capacity, but internal power design and cooling constraints are emerging as key bottlenecks. Industry observers warn that grid limitations and facility-level engineering hurdles could slow the buildout.
stories.why_it_matters: The gap between announced capacity and deliverable power is becoming the defining constraint on Korea's AI infrastructure ambitions. Developers, utilities, and equipment suppliers all face pressure to resolve power distribution and cooling design issues before projects can move from announcement to operation.
stories.content:
The South Korean government's announcement that it will build 8.4 gigawatts (GW) of artificial intelligence (AI) data center capacity by 2029 has made power procurement the central challenge. Experts say the bottleneck lies not only in where and how electricity is sourced, but also in how that power is distributed and cooled once inside the data center.

In June, the government unveiled its "Three Mega Projects for South Korea's Great Leap Forward," committing to a first phase of 8.4GW of AI data center capacity, including 5GW from SK, 2.4GW from GS, and 1GW from Naver. The long-term plan calls for expanding total capacity to 18.4GW, with support for power and water supply, site diversification, and demonstration of South Korean-made power and cooling solutions.

What sets AI data centers apart from conventional ones is the rapid escalation in power draw per server rack. A server rack is a bundle of servers containing GPUs, central processing units (CPUs), memory, and storage. Under existing low-voltage power architectures, as rack power grows, so do current, heat, and power-loss burdens. This is why observers argue that both the external grid running from power plants to the data center and the internal power delivery path from the data center to the GPU—the so-called "electric highway"—must be validated together.

### The 1MW-per-Rack Era and the Limits of 48V Architecture

Lee Jeong-ho, a professor of mechanical engineering at Ajou University, said, "These days Nvidia doesn't sell GPU chips one by one—it sells them as racks. Current AI server racks draw roughly 150kW, the next generation will reach 600kW, and in the long term a single rack could scale to 1MW."

The 48V power architecture widely used in server racks today offers the advantages of familiarity and safety due to its low voltage. But when transmitting the same amount of power, lower voltage means higher current. Supplying 100kW to a single rack requires more than 2,000 amps under a 48V design. As rack power grows to 600kW and 1MW, even greater current is needed, compounding wiring, thermal, and power-loss burdens.

A paper published last month on the preprint server arXiv flagged the same issue. An international research team including Lee Sang-hwi, a professor at Korea University, analyzed how the growth in AI workloads is increasing data center power demand, instantaneous current swings, and thermal stress, and concluded that the existing 48V server rack architecture and low-voltage AC distribution could hit their limits.

The researchers proposed alternatives including raising intra-rack voltage to 400V or 800V, shifting data center internal distribution to a DC-centric model, and connecting the grid to the data center via medium-voltage solid-state transformers. Solid-state transformers use more power electronics than conventional transformers to finely control voltage conversion and power flow. Higher voltage allows the same power to be delivered at lower current, while DC distribution reduces conversion stages and cuts losses.

However, these design shifts still require further research and demonstration. Because data centers must run around the clock without interruption, deploying high-voltage DC distribution demands validation of where to interrupt power during faults, how to prevent electric shock and fire, how to handle grounding, and whether the system remains stable over long-term operation. The researchers themselves identified protection and fault response, grounding, standardization, long-term reliability, co-design of thermal and electrical systems, and digital twin-based verification as the key bottlenecks for next-generation power architectures.

### Cooling Technology Must Be Redesigned in Tandem

When the electric highway of an AI data center changes, thermal management must change with it, because a substantial share of GPU power consumption is converted to heat. Professor Lee explained, "GPUs generally need to operate below roughly 85 degrees Celsius to deliver full performance, and as power consumption rises, so does heat. It's the same principle as a phone getting hot after prolonged use."

Conventional data centers have primarily relied on air cooling, blowing cold air into server rooms to extract heat. But as AI server power draw climbs, the center of gravity in cooling is shifting from air to liquid. Liquid cooling circulates water or dielectric coolant close to the chip to remove heat, transferring it far more efficiently than air.

As next-generation AI chips consume even more power, cooling devices must move closer to the chip—and ultimately inside the chip or semiconductor package. Kim Sung-jin, a professor of mechanical engineering at KAIST, said, "Liquid cooling is already in use, but companies like Intel and HP are developing technologies to embed cooling devices inside the chip itself. The technology isn't mature yet, so it will take time. Integrating multiple chips and cooling devices at scale is not easy."

Whether South Korea can actually validate new power delivery and cooling architectures is another variable. An AI data center is not a facility where server racks, power supplies, and cooling units can be swapped out independently. Power delivery and cooling hardware are attached according to the rack architecture defined by the server manufacturer.

Professor Lee Jeong-ho said, "South Korea says it's building AI data centers, but the core is missing. We can produce the component technologies needed for cooling, but there is no company in South Korea that builds complete systems or server and rack technology." He added, "Even if we actually set up an AI data center, it is nearly impossible right now to configure it the way we want."

### External Grid and Transmission Timelines Are Also Wild Cards

The power grid challenges outside the AI data center remain as well. Researchers at the University of Calgary in Canada have analyzed how the rapid proliferation of AI data centers amplifies not just total power demand but also issues of location, timing, and power variability. If data center loads concentrate in specific regions, they could outpace the expansion of clean energy, while grid flexibility, reliability, and carbon emissions concerns grow in tandem.

Lee Yu-soo, a professor in the Department of Energy Policy and Technology Convergence at Soongsil University, also cautioned that plans to use renewable energy from South Korea's Honam region for AI data centers should be viewed carefully. "AI training workloads require large-scale GPUs running simultaneously, so power must be supplied stably 24 hours a day," he said. "It won't be easy unless renewable energy is combined with sources like nuclear or liquefied natural gas (LNG)."

Transmission grid construction speed is another variable. Professor Lee said, "South Korea has many long-distance transmission arrangements from power plants, so the pace of transmission grid construction is critical. Transmission projects come with community acceptance issues, costs, and schedule delays." He added, "It's uncertain whether data center commissioning and power supply timelines will align. The whole picture needs to be re-examined."

stories.title: Korean engineers turn to the deep sea for data centers
stories.summary: South Korean engineers are exploring underwater data center concepts, placing facilities in the deep sea as a way to address cooling and land constraints. The approach follows similar experiments by Microsoft and others with submerged server deployments.
stories.why_it_matters: If viable, subsea facilities could ease two of Korea's most pressing data center constraints at once — land scarcity and cooling costs. The research positions Korean engineering firms at the front of an experimental deployment model that, if proven, could alter site-selection economics across coastal APAC markets.
stories.content:
A small Korean coastal city could soon host up to 100,000 AI servers

- **Ulsan is testing underwater data centers to support growing AI workloads**
- **The project carries a KRW 51.1 billion (about $37 million) budget through 2030**
- **Seawater could provide cooling without conventional mechanical refrigeration systems**

South Korean city Ulsan is exploring underwater infrastructure as AI computing continues to strain land availability, power grids, and cooling systems nationwide.

The city is partnering with the Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology (KIOST) to design a standardized subsea data center model.

Officials hope the approach can ease some of the site and cooling constraints that conventional data centers increasingly face across the country.

## Building a standardized underwater model

The partnership between Ulsan and KIOST runs through 2030, with a combined budget of KRW 51.1 billion (about $37 million) - KRW 40 billion (about $29 million) of which comes directly from the central government, with the remainder covered locally.

“Ulsan plans to complete the standard model by 2030 and begin developing an underwater data-center complex for commercialization from 2031,” the city said.

The goal is a working, carbon-neutral template for underwater computing that other sites could later replicate.

The project will take place in waters roughly 20 meters deep off the Ulsan coastline, where engineers plan to rely on seawater — which averages about 13.3°C annually — as a core part of the cooling strategy.

Researchers intend to combine pressure-resistant vessel design with hybrid cooling systems described as ultra-high-efficiency by project planners.

Server units and power distribution equipment will follow standardized modular designs meant to simplify future scaling.

The team is aiming for an operating efficiency of approximately PUE 1.2 once testing concludes.

SK Telecom joined the partnership in January 2026, taking on responsibility for GPU-based infrastructure and server operations management.

In addition to Ulsan and KIOST, other research organizations, academics and industry professionals are part of the project working behind the scenes.

Their combined role covers everything from vessel engineering to the software layer that will eventually manage AI workloads underwater.

## A larger commercial vision

A separate, longer-term concept discussed by the city involves roughly KRW 500 billion (about $360 million) in investment and capacity for up to 100,000 servers.

This larger sum is not tied to the current phase of work and only reflects what a full commercial buildout could eventually cost.

Whether Ulsan reaches that scale will depend entirely on how the initial testing phase performs.

South Korea faces mounting pressure to expand computing capacity as AI workloads multiply across chipmakers, cloud providers, and research institutions nationwide.

Land near major population centers remains scarce and expensive, pushing planners toward unconventional sites away from crowded urban areas.

Ocean water offers a cooling resource that requires none of the mechanical refrigeration conventional facilities depend on heavily.

If the Ulsan demonstration performs as expected, similar underwater sites could eventually spread along other stretches of Korea's coastline.

For now, the ocean floor represents a promising but unproven answer to Korea's expanding AI infrastructure demands.

stories.title: NVIDIA invests $1 billion in NAVER to expand South Korea AI data center capacity
stories.summary: NVIDIA has committed a $1 billion investment in South Korean tech company NAVER to expand AI data center capacity in the country. The deal deepens ties between the chipmaker and one of Korea's leading cloud and AI platform operators.
stories.why_it_matters: The investment accelerates South Korea's bid to become a regional AI compute hub and gives NAVER the capital and hardware alignment to scale sovereign AI infrastructure. For the broader APAC market, it signals that chip vendors are increasingly willing to fund capacity buildouts directly, reshaping how large AI data center projects get financed.

Nvidia Corp invests $1 billion in NAVER Corp via share issuance to expand the GAK Sejong AI datacenter to 200 megawatts by 2028. Nvidia will supply GPUs for the facility, with Brookfield Asset Management proposing up to $9 billion in additional funding. The deal follows previous partnerships with SK Hynix and SK Telecom, strengthening Nvidia's AI ecosystem in South Korea.

*this image is generated using AI for illustrative purposes only.

Nvidia Corp has agreed to invest approximately $1 billion in NAVER Corp, marking a significant expansion of its artificial intelligence footprint in South Korea. Announced on Saturday during South Korean President Lee Jae Myung’s visit to the AI Summit in San Francisco, the deal aims to scale up local AI computing capacity. The investment will see Nvidia acquire 7.2 million newly issued shares of NAVER at 204,500 KRW ($139.45) per share, representing a roughly 1% discount to NAVER’s Friday closing price.

The capital injection is primarily directed toward expanding NAVER’s GAK Sejong AI datacenter. The facility’s capacity is set to grow from 55 megawatts to 200 megawatts by 2028. In a regulatory filing on Monday, NAVER clarified the partnership structure, noting that Nvidia will participate as a supplier of GPUs rather than as an equity partner sharing revenue and business risks. This structural adjustment defines Nvidia’s role strictly within the hardware supply chain for the expanded infrastructure.

Brookfield Asset Management Ltd is also involved in the broader infrastructure push, proposing up to $9 billion to fund the AI infrastructure development. This substantial financial backing underscores the scale of the upcoming deployment. The expanded facility is expected to deploy next-generation Vera Rubin and Blackwell systems, providing production-scale AI computing capacity for enterprises, startups, and government organizations across the region.

This transaction builds upon a partnership announced in June, where NAVER committed to using Nvidia technology for AI data center expansion and industrial AI applications. That earlier announcement also highlighted Nvidia’s broader ecosystem partnerships in South Korea with SK Hynix, SK Telecom, and Doosan. The current deal solidifies Nvidia’s strategic position in the country’s rapidly growing AI sector.

Market reaction reflected the positive sentiment surrounding the deal. In Seoul, NAVER shares rose 7.23% to 222,500 KRW ($151.76) at the time of writing. Meanwhile, Nvidia’s shares closed 0.92% lower on Friday at $206.84, dipping another 0.02% in extended trading. The divergence in immediate stock performance highlights the distinct market dynamics affecting each entity despite the collaborative nature of the announcement.

## What the Numbers Show

The shift in partnership structure is a critical detail for investors analyzing Nvidia’s exposure in Asia. By moving from a risk-sharing partner model to a pure GPU supplier role, Nvidia secures high-margin hardware sales while limiting its operational liability in the datacenter’s long-term performance. The $1 billion equity stake ensures alignment with NAVER’s success, but the primary revenue driver will likely be the volume of Vera Rubin and Blackwell systems deployed in the 200-megawatt facility. With Brookfield proposing up to $9 billion in additional funding, the total capital pool for this single regional initiative suggests a massive scale of infrastructure development, potentially setting a template for future AI hub expansions in other Asian markets.

How might Nvidia's shift to a pure supplier role in this deal influence its future partnership structures with other Asian tech giants?

What impact could the deployment of 200 megawatts of AI capacity by 2028 have on South Korea's competitive standing in the global semiconductor and AI infrastructure market?

Will the proposed $9 billion from Brookfield Asset Management set a new benchmark for private equity involvement in sovereign-level AI infrastructure projects?
